item.title: When Family Wounds Run Deep: Understanding Moral Injury Between Siblings
item.description:
Sibling relationships are often thought of as one of the most enduring connections in our lives. It’s the connection with people who shared a childhood bedroom, a dinner table, and defining moments of growing up. But for many adults, this bond with a sibling carries something more complicated than nostalgia. The violation of deeply held values by a sibling causes serious harm and erodes the sense of safety that a family is meant to provide. The result is a wound described as moral injury.

This phenomenon goes deeper than a case of hurt feelings after a disagreement. Moral injury is the serious psychological damage that occurs when a person experiences something that fundamentally violates their moral framework. This type of wound in a sibling relationship can be disorienting as it strikes the core of family identity and belonging.

This type of pain requires compassionate attention, psychologically and spiritually. The complexity of these wounds rarely resolves without intentional support.

What Moral Injury Looks Like Between Siblings

The concept of moral injury gained recognition through research on veterans returning from combat. This was a framework for understanding what happens psychologically when people encounter events that violate their core beliefs of right and wrong. Mental health professionals are now recognizing that the same framework applies across a range of relationship settings, including the family.

This kind of wound between siblings can take many forms. It could come from a brother who stood by while abuse occurred or a sister who manipulated family resources and spread harmful lies that caused lasting damage to another’s reputation or life. It could have been a sibling who broke a sacred confidence shared in a moment of deep vulnerability. These offenses are not minor or ordinary family friction.

These are the events that alter the lens through which an injured person sees themselves, their family, and their place in the world. The damage lasts long after the event and involves the collapse of a trusted reality and a profound loss of the relationship. This kind of rupture in a family relationship deserves serious attention and should be handled with the care it requires.

For help, we can go to God. “The Lord is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.” (Psalm 9:9, ESV) This reminds us of God’s faithfulness to us in even the hardest times of betrayal and mistrust.

The Hidden Weight Siblings Carry Alone

The most painful aspect of this situation is how invisible the hurt remains. Society has an expectation that can leave individuals who were harmed by a sibling feeling confused, ashamed, and as if their pain does not matter. Extended family or friends may offer advice during these moments, suggesting that the individual move on, but such responses can deepen the sense of isolation rather than ease it.

The individual who was harmed is trying to process the original event and grieve the relationship they believed they had. They are mourning the family they believed was the true version. This grief is heavy and complex and does not resolve quickly. What especially adds to difficulty is that sibling pain often lacks the social recognition that other losses receive.

There is no clear ritual for grieving a broken sibling bond, the way there is for other kinds of loss. This can leave a person feeling as though their pain is somehow invalid or excessive. It is important to recognize that individuals may need more than encouragement to forgive and to navigate this kind of deep pain. These individuals need an honest, supportive space to name what happened and understand what it has truly cost.

How Moral Injury Between Siblings Affects Mental Health

If the pain of sibling betrayal goes untreated, it will affect mental health significantly over time. Many individuals who carry these unresolved wounds may experience some symptoms that closely resemble Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.

People who experience moral injury could develop intrusive thoughts, emotional numbness, and a persistent sense of shame or self-blame related to the loss of a relationship due to an event that crossed a line. Some of these individuals may quietly question whether they deserve connection at all. In contrast, others develop deep patterns of distrust in their marriages, friendships, and even in their approaches to parenting.

Features of depression and anxiety can be common companions to this kind of loss. There is an unrelenting awareness that something fundamentally wrong happened and that people who should’ve cared did not. The result is an erosion of the person’s sense of worth and safety across many years.

Research in the field of relational trauma points to the fact that unresolved wounds from close family relationships can also surface in physical ways. These include disrupted sleep, chronic fatigue, and a diminished ability to regulate emotions in everyday situations. The body often holds what the mind has not yet fully processed.

Finding the proper support in these relational traumas will help in understanding the layered nature of this pain and offer care that addresses the emotional and spiritual dimensions of the pain the individual is facing. Connecting specifically with a Christian counselor can remind people how to come to Jesus as described in Matthew:

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, ESV 

Navigating the Journey Toward Healing

Healing from this type of pain does not follow a straight line, nor does it always end in reconciliation. Some individuals find their journey toward wholeness means rebuilding a sense of personal identity damaged by betrayal. For others, it requires learning to grieve the lost relationship and the family they hoped for. Either way, the process asks something significant of the person who was hurt. It asks them to hold space for grief and growth at the same time, which is no small thing.

Christian counseling offers a structured and safe environment where those emotions can be worked through honestly without judgment. This type of counseling can also incorporate trauma-informed therapy, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, and spiritually integrated counseling. Together, these approaches can help individuals work through complex relational pain.

The goal is to help individuals navigate moral injury by integrating their experience in ways that allow them to live more freely, form healthier connections, and discover a stable sense of self. Healing is the process that deserves skilled, compassionate, and constant support over time.

Hope for Healing

Sibling relationships are among the most formative in an individual’s life. When these relationships become a source of harm, the impact can linger for decades. Sibling betrayal pain is not something to dismiss or minimize. It is a serious form of psychological injury that touches areas of identity, faith, and sense of belonging.

No one should have to navigate that alone or carry the weight of a wound they were never meant to carry. Many people carry it silently for years, or sometimes decades. They move through life wondering why certain relationships feel impossible or why trust never quite settles. The connection between those patterns and an old sibling wound is often the last thing they consider examining.

Healing begins with honest acknowledgment supported by professional care and grounded in the truth that God does not abandon people in the depths of their pain. Reaching out for help regarding the aftermath of sibling betrayal is a meaningful and courageous act of self-respect. It is a step toward cultivating the wholeness you deserve.

If you are facing difficulty with pain related to moral injury from a sibling, reach out to a Christian counselor who understands the complexity of family pain to get you started on your way to healing.

item.title: Anxiety: When Imagination is the Enemy
item.description:
We all love a good fairy tale. Mythical lands, strange and exotic creatures, and magical powers that can solve every problem from the mundane to the severe. But imagination, with all its sparkle and shine, can actually be to your detriment when you have anxiety.

Anxiety is sometimes hard to understand or communicate because it doesn’t usually come from what can be physically confirmed. In other words, it doesn’t stem from what is actually happening or what others can readily see or understand. Most of the time, anxiety comes from what could happen in the future.

Anxiety leverages your God-given creativity and sends you into an imaginary land of extreme and negative future outcomes that is convincingly real.

An Overachieving Imagination

People with anxiety are often highly perceptive, creative, emotionally aware, and future-oriented thinkers. Anxiety hijacks your brain’s natural warning system and wreaks confusion. The same inventive mental ability that allows someone to envision possibilities is also pretty creative when it comes to conjuring up future catastrophes. You’ve heard the idiom “too much of a good thing.” This can be said about your imagination, too.

Your God-given creativity is a blessing most of the time. But your ability to think about the future in realistic detail can make things tricky. When paired with your imagination, which is capable of complex thinking and multilayered scenarios, this creativity can feel like it is working against you if you suffer from anxiety.

As your anxiety creates fictitious future scenarios, your brain begins to react to them as if they’re real, which starts a chain reaction. When your brain doesn’t accept these images and ideas as creative works of fiction but as authentic and urgent warnings, a process begins. Your brain signals your body to be on high alert. Muscles begin to tighten, the heart begins to race, and soon you’re fully in crisis mode over something that isn’t real.

When Thoughts Spiral

The problem doesn’t lie in the imagination itself. Imagination is one of the greatest gifts God gave us. It’s what allows authors to write novels, musicians to compose songs, and inventors to create new things. Imagination helps you do more than create, too. It is what allows you to empathize, solve problems, and add beauty to the world around you.

Anxiety takes that beautiful gift and weaponizes it for its own good and purpose. It doesn’t adhere to normal, reasonable boundaries. Instead of your imagination being directed by truth and reality, it becomes directed by fear. Through the clouded and convoluted lens of anxiety, an unanswered text can suddenly become evidence that something is wrong with a relationship. One unfamiliar symptom turns into a terrifying diagnosis.

Unfortunately, the anxious mind doesn’t just stop with one possibility. It keeps building, one tragic brick at a time. It pushes you to think about what will happen next and next and next, never being satisfied with the most likely cause, explanation, or outcome. You convince yourself that one minuscule situation or weak piece of evidence is proof that you’re surely heading for doom.

Because your body responds to these imagined dangers as if they are real, anxiety can become physically exhausting. Your nervous system goes into survival mode, responding as if the threat were real and imminent, to situations that only exist within your imagination.

Reclaiming Your Imagination

Anxiety uses your creative mind to pull you out of the present moment and thrust you into a tragic future. It forces you to mentally discard reason, logic, and real evidence and live in that imagined future as if it were the present reality. But if imagination is a God-given gift being abused unrightly, surely that imagination can be recaptured and used for good.

Taking Your Thoughts Captive

Scripture tells us to “…take every thought captive to obey Christ,” (2 Corinthians 10:5, ESV). That verse, while widely retold, is still underrated because it really is an important key to overcoming anxiety.

The words sound so simple, but in reality, they offer a very profound, life-changing idea. It is not always an easy one to execute because we have an inherent tendency to trust ourselves. While you are likely to trust the thoughts in your own head, not every thought that enters is deserving.

Jesus was obviously aware of the human tendency to borrow future trouble. “Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.” (Matthew 6:34, NIV) The advice Jesus offers may have been given in the Sermon on the Mount thousands of years ago, but His advice is still applicable today. Try the following strategies to heed Jesus’ advice.

  • Set Daily Boundaries: In the Lord’s Prayer, there is a request for daily bread. Not weekly or monthly bread, but daily. When your mind starts to spiral toward what might happen a month from now or what life will look like in a year, actively pull yourself back to what is happening in the next 24 hours. Ask yourself what you need to do in the next few hours, not what might happen in the future.
  • Control Only the Controllable: Much of your anxiety can come from trying to control things that are simply outside of your authority to control. You can’t control the economy or other people’s opinions or an unexpected health event, so stop trying.

To help take your thoughts captive, draw two columns on a piece of paper. Write down everything that’s driving your anxiety and put what you can actually do something about today into one column. You can write that apology email today, but you can’t restore an entire relationship, for example. In the second column, write down those things that you can’t control and hand that column in its entirety over to God.

  • Curate Your Media: We live in an information-saturated world. Through modern media, we are exposed to more global tragedy than any other generation has experienced, and that is partially responsible for why anxiety is rising. But you don’t have to allow negative input into your life unfiltered. Establish a routine that doesn’t include doomscrolling and protect the first and last thirty minutes of your day from email or news.
  • Feed Yourself Scripture: If you feed your soul with Scripture, you will find peace. The Word has a unique ability to bring peace into even the most tense situations. Take time to read Scripture. Memorize key verses. And when your mind starts to travel to uncertain and dangerous places, latch onto the Scriptures to help guide you back to center.
  • Seek Therapy: While taking your thoughts captive can be a spiritual practice to help anxiety, some anxiety stems from biological factors or past trauma. Seeking therapy can be another way to help take your thoughts captive. If you’re struggling with intrusive or unbridled repetitive thoughts or symptoms of generalized anxiety, therapy can help.

Through therapeutic practices like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), you can learn to spot cognitive distortions, which are essentially the fiction-writing techniques that your anxiety uses to make imagined disasters feel like imminent reality.

Rewriting Your Creative Parts

Taking your thoughts captive doesn’t mean that you have to shut your imagination down entirely, but it does require you to reassign the authorship. Anxiety wants you to believe that you are the sole author and authority of your future. It wants you to envision a future where you are helpless and living in the worst possible version of it. The good news is that as a child of God, you’re not the one writing your future at all, and neither is your anxiety.

A Bright Future

Imagine what could happen if that same vibrant, deep-thinking mind of yours was allowed to envision good possibilities instead of catastrophic and tragic ones. The same mental capacity that can map out disaster scenarios is also capable of imagining what life could look like with God’s goodness overtaking it.

If you would like support in navigating your imagination and anxiety, please contact Joseph Bennett to schedule an appointment with a licensed Christian therapist. A Christian therapist can help you take your thoughts captive, find peace amid anxious moments, and transform your thoughts into hopeful dreams of a beautiful future guided by God.

item.title: Most Common Symptoms of Depression: How to Know If You’re Depressed
item.description:
When most people picture depression, they might think it is someone who is deeply sad. Maybe they frequently cry, struggle to get out of bed, or struggle to keep up with everyday responsibilities. Sometimes depression does look like that. But other times it can look completely different.

Depression can look like going to work every day but feeling exhausted by the time you get home. It can look like snapping at the people you love and not understanding why everything irritates you lately. It can look like canceling plans, ignoring text messages, or spending more and more time alone. It can even look like a person who appears to have everything together on the outside.

This is one reason depression can often go unnoticed for a prolonged period. People may recognize that something feels different, but because they aren’t experiencing overwhelming sadness, they don’t even consider that they could be dealing with depression.

Understanding the symptoms, especially the ones that are easier to miss, can help you recognize when it might be time to reach out for support.

So, what is depression?

Everyone experiences sadness, disappointment, grief, and difficult seasons. Feeling sad does not automatically mean that you are depressed. Clinical depression, often called Major Depressive Disorder, involves a collection of symptoms that persist and begin affecting how you think, feel, and function.

Depression can influence your emotions, motivation, relationships, sleep, appetite, concentration, energy, and even the way you see yourself. For some people, depression develops after a significant loss or stressful life event. For others, there isn’t an obvious explanation. You may even find yourself thinking, “Why do I feel this way? Nothing is really wrong,” but not having an obvious reason for your symptoms doesn’t make them less real.

What are the most common symptoms of depression?

Depression doesn’t look exactly the same for everyone. However, several symptoms are commonly associated with it.

Persistent Sadness or Emptiness

You may feel sad more days than not, but depression can also feel like emptiness. Instead of crying constantly, you might feel flat, disconnected, or emotionally numb. Sometimes you don’t feel sad; you just don’t feel like yourself anymore.

Losing Interest in Things You Used to Enjoy

One of the most important symptoms of depression is called anhedonia, which means losing interest or pleasure in things you previously enjoyed. You may still participate in activities because you know you are supposed to, but they don’t feel the same anymore.

Dinner with friends feels like work. Your hobbies sit untouched. Family activities feel like something you need to get through instead of something you enjoy. Your life may look similar from the outside while feeling different internally.

Changes in Sleep

Depression can affect sleep in opposite ways. Some people struggle to fall asleep, wake frequently during the night, or wake much earlier than they want to. Others find themselves sleeping significantly more than usual. You may sleep eight or nine hours and still wake up feeling exhausted.

Changes in Appetite

You might notice that you’re eating much more or much less than usual. Food may become a source of comfort, or you may simply lose interest in eating. Significant changes in appetite or weight can sometimes accompany depression.

Low Energy

Depression can make ordinary tasks feel unusually difficult. Getting dressed, answering an email, making dinner, cleaning the house, or returning a phone call may require more energy than they once did. This isn’t necessarily laziness or a lack of discipline. When someone is experiencing depression, motivation and energy can be significantly affected.

Difficulty Concentrating or Making Decisions

You might reread the same paragraph several times. You walk into a room and forget why you went there. You struggle to follow conversations or make decisions that normally wouldn’t bother you. Even small choices can feel overwhelming. What should we have for dinner? What should I wear? Which email should I answer first?

Depression Symptoms People Often Miss

Some symptoms of depression are less obvious and may be mistaken for stress, personality changes, or simply being overwhelmed.

Irritability

Depression doesn’t always show up as sadness. Sometimes it shows up as anger. You might have less patience with your children, feel constantly frustrated with your spouse, or become irritated by things that normally wouldn’t bother you. If you find yourself thinking, “Why is everyone getting on my nerves lately?”, it may be worth paying attention to what else is happening emotionally.

Withdrawing From People

Withdrawal can happen gradually. You stop initiating plans. You let calls go to voicemail. You respond to fewer texts. You tell yourself you’re tired and would rather stay home. Eventually, you may realize that your world has become much smaller.

Feeling Numb

Some people with depression don’t describe themselves as sad at all – they describe feeling nothing. You may know intellectually that something should make you happy, excited, or emotional, but you can’t seem to access the feeling. That emotional numbness can be just as important to notice as sadness.

Increased Guilt and Self-Criticism

Depression often changes the way people talk to themselves.

  • “I’m failing.”
  • “I’m a terrible parent.”
  • “Everyone else handles life better than I do.”
  • “I’m a burden.”
  • “I should be able to get myself together.”

These thoughts can begin to feel like facts rather than symptoms.

Physical Symptoms

Depression doesn’t only affect your thoughts and emotions. It can also show up physically. Some people experience headaches, digestive issues, unexplained aches and pains, heaviness, fatigue, or other physical discomfort. When medical explanations don’t fully account for ongoing symptoms, emotional health may be another piece worth exploring.

“But I’m Still Functioning. Could I Really Be Depressed?”

This is one of the biggest reasons people overlook depression.

You may think:

  • “I still go to work.”
  • “I’m taking care of my kids.”
  • “I still show up at church.”
  • “I’m getting things done.”
  • “I’m not lying in bed all day.”

So, you assume you can’t be depressed, but functioning and struggling can exist at the same time. Some people become quite skilled at pushing through. They meet deadlines, take care of everyone else, attend activities, smile when they’re supposed to, and continue fulfilling their responsibilities, then they get home and collapse. Or they realize they don’t actually enjoy any of the life they’re working so hard to maintain.

Instead of asking only, “Am I functioning?”, it may be more helpful to ask, “How much energy does it take for me to keep functioning?”, and “Do I still feel connected to the life I’m living?” You don’t have to reach the point where you can’t function before your emotional health deserves attention.

Depression and Faith: “Why do I feel so far from God?”

For Christians, depression can sometimes create another layer of confusion.

You may wonder:

  • Why can’t I feel God’s presence?
  • Shouldn’t I have more joy?
  • If I trusted God more, would I still feel this way?

Depression is not automatically evidence of weak faith. Scripture doesn’t hide emotional suffering. In Psalm 42, the psalmist repeatedly describes his soul as “downcast.” He acknowledges his distress while continuing to turn toward God.

We see another powerful example in 1 Kings 19. After an incredibly intense period in Elijah’s life, he becomes exhausted, overwhelmed, and hopeless. God doesn’t begin by criticizing Elijah for not having enough faith. Instead, Elijah is allowed to sleep. He is given food. He rests. And God continues meeting him in his distress. There is something important in that picture.

Sometimes caring for our emotional and physical needs is part of how we walk through a difficult season with God. Psalm 34:18 tells us that the Lord is close to the brokenhearted. God’s nearness isn’t dependent upon our ability to feel it perfectly. Depression can change the way you experience God’s presence without changing the reality of God’s presence.

Faith and professional mental health support don’t have to compete with one another. Counseling, healthy relationships, medical care when appropriate, prayer, Scripture, rest, and practical coping skills can all have a place in healing.

When should I get help for depression?

If several of these symptoms have been present consistently, are getting worse, or are beginning to interfere with your relationships, work, responsibilities, or ability to enjoy life, it may be time to talk with a mental health professional. You don’t need to wait until things become unbearable.

Depression is treatable. Counseling can help you better understand what you’re experiencing, identify patterns that may be contributing to your symptoms, develop healthier coping skills, and begin reconnecting with the parts of life that have started to feel distant.

And if depression includes thoughts about death, suicide, self-harm, or feeling that others would be better off without you, those thoughts should always be taken seriously and deserve immediate support.

You don’t have to wait until you’re falling apart

Depression doesn’t always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it slowly changes the way you experience your life. You may still be working, still parenting, still showing up, still praying, still getting things done, but you don’t feel like yourself anymore. That matters.

If you recognize yourself in some of these symptoms, consider reaching out for support. You don’t have to wait until you can no longer function to decide that you’re ready to feel better.

If you’re wondering whether depression may be affecting your life, reach out today to schedule a counseling appointment. Together, we can begin understanding what you’re experiencing and take the next steps toward healing and hope.

item.title: Understanding the Types of Grief: Why Grief Does Not Always Look the Way We Expect
item.description:
Grief is something every person will experience at some point in life. But although grief is universal, the way we experience it is deeply personal. Two people can experience a similar loss and respond in different ways.

One person may return to work quickly and appear to be doing relatively well. Another may have difficulty sleeping, concentrating, working, or connecting with others. One person may cry often, while another may feel numb. None of these responses automatically mean that someone is grieving the “right” or “wrong” way.

Grief can affect our emotions, bodies, relationships, routines, faith, and sense of who we are. It can also change over time. You may feel okay one day and find yourself overwhelmed by sadness the next. You may experience a mix of anger, guilt, relief, loneliness, anxiety, or even moments of genuine happiness.

If you have been wondering whether your grief is normal, it may help you to know that there is no single way grief is supposed to look.

Grief, Loss, and Bereavement: What is the difference?

The words grief, loss, and bereavement are often used interchangeably, but they describe different parts of the experience.

Loss refers to what has been taken away or changed. Loss may involve the death of a loved one, but it can also involve the end of a marriage, the loss of a job, a change in health or physical ability, infertility, a move, estrangement, financial security, or an important role or identity.

Grief is the emotional response to that loss. It can include sadness, anger, guilt, confusion, yearning, anxiety, numbness, relief, loneliness, or even moments when you feel surprisingly okay.

Bereavement most specifically refers to the experience of losing someone through death.

Although grief is often associated with death, we can grieve many kinds of losses. This is one reason there can be diverse types of grief.

Grief is not limited to the death of a loved one

When we hear the word grief, most of us think about losing someone we love. The death of a parent, spouse, child, sibling, friend, or another loved one can certainly bring profound grief.

You may grieve the end of a marriage or relationship. You may grieve a career that once gave you purpose or identity. You may grieve a change in your health, physical abilities, or independence. Parents may experience grief as their children grow older and leave home. You may even grieve a former version of yourself – the person you were before a major life event changed your circumstances.

These losses may not always receive the same recognition as a death, but that does not make them insignificant. The meaning we attach to what we have lost often plays a key role in how deeply that loss is experienced.

The Five Stages of Grief: A Framework, Not a Formula

You may have heard of the five stages of grief: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. These stages are associated with psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross. They have become a familiar way of talking about grief and bereavement. However, it is important not to interpret these stages as a strict, linear roadmap that every grieving person must follow.

Grief does not necessarily move from denial to anger, then bargaining, depression, and finally acceptance. You may experience several of these emotions at the same time. You may move between them, revisit them, or experience emotions that do not fit into any of the five categories.

For some people, the stages simply provide useful language for experiences associated with grief, but they should not become a standard to use to decide whether you are grieving “correctly.”

Different Ways Grief Can Show Up

There is no single way to experience grief, and there is no single list to capture every person’s grief. The circumstances surrounding a loss can influence how grief unfolds, and different experiences can overlap. The following are some common types of grief that may help put into words various experiences.

Anticipatory Grief

Anticipatory grief is when someone begins grieving before a loss has actually happened. This can happen when someone you love has a terminal or progressive illness, or when you know that a significant change or loss is coming.

For example, a family member may grieve changes as they watch a loved one’s health decline, knowing that the relationship and family life may never be the same. Anticipatory grief can bring sadness, fear, anxiety, anger, and even guilt for grieving while the person you love is still here.

Disenfranchised Grief

Disenfranchised grief refers to grief that feels unrecognized, unsupported, or socially difficult to express. You may feel that others do not understand why the loss matters or may even question whether you have a “right” to grieve.

This can happen after the death of someone who was not considered immediate family, the loss of a former partner, an estrangement, infertility, miscarriage, or another loss that people may minimize. When people around you don’t recognize your loss, you may minimize it yourself, which can make grief especially lonely.

Traumatic Grief

Grief can also be complicated by trauma. A sudden, violent, frightening, or unexpected death may leave someone grieving the person they lost while also trying to process what happened. You may experience intrusive memories, heightened anxiety, difficulty feeling safe, or intense distress surrounding reminders of the event. In these situations, the grief may involve both the loss itself and the traumatic circumstances surrounding it.

Delayed Grief

Delayed grief refers to a grief response that does not fully show up immediately following a loss. Sometimes a person initially needs to focus on practical responsibilities, support other family members, manage a crisis, or simply get through the immediate aftermath. They may not feel like there is room to grieve.

Then weeks, months, or even years later, the emotions become more noticeable. A seemingly unrelated event can sometimes bring feelings connected to an earlier loss. Grief that appears later does not necessarily mean someone did not care enough when the loss happened. Sometimes we recognize the weight of what happened when we finally have the space or capacity to process it.

Ambiguous Loss

Psychologist Pauline Boss used the term ambiguous loss to describe losses that lack clarity or closure that usually comes with a more defined loss.

For example, a family caring for a loved one with dementia may grieve changes in the person they once knew while continuing to care for the person who is physically present. Estrangement can also create this kind of grief. The relationship may have ended or changed, but the person is still alive and may still be important to you. These situations can be particularly difficult because there may not be a clear ending or answer about what comes next.

Is there such a thing as “normal” grief?

People commonly ask how long they are supposed to grieve. Some people experience intense grief initially and gradually regain their ability to function. Others experience grief in waves. Certain days may feel manageable while others bring a sudden return of sadness.

Grief does not always mean “getting over” something. It is possible for a significant loss to still become part of your story and part of you without controlling every aspect of your future. This distinction matters. Healing does not mean forgetting. Moving forward does not mean leaving someone behind. Feeling joy again does not mean that the loss mattered less.

How do I make grief better?

This question is understandable. When grief hurts, it is natural to want to make it stop. Rather than approaching grief as something that needs to be eliminated, it may be more helpful to ask: What meaning can I make of an experience that has changed my life? How do I learn to live with what has happened?

Counseling can provide a space to explore these questions without being rushed toward a predetermined answer. You can talk honestly about sadness, anger, guilt, regret, loneliness, relief, fear, or uncertainty without being told that you should already be doing better.

Therapy can also help with the practical consequences of loss. A significant loss can change your routines, relationships, responsibilities, identity, and plans for the future. Therapy may help you rebuild daily routines, communicate with family members, prepare for difficult anniversaries or reminders, strengthen your support system, and develop ways of coping with emotions that feel overwhelming.

The goal is not to erase the loss. The goal is to make room for the pain of what happened while continuing to build and live a meaningful life.

How can Christian counseling help with grief?

For Christians, grief may affect more than emotional well-being. It can also affect your spiritual walk and the way you understand your faith. You may find comfort in your faith while simultaneously experiencing doubt, anger, confusion, or questions about God. Having those questions does not necessarily mean that you have lost your faith.

Scripture does not present grief as something that believers are expected to hide. One of the clearest examples is found in John 11. When Jesus encountered Mary and Martha after the death of their brother Lazarus, Jesus wept. He knew what was about to happen, yet He still entered into the sorrow of the people who were grieving.

It reminds us that faith and grief are not necessarily opposites. For some people, faith becomes an important source of hope as they learn to live with what cannot be changed. That hope does not require pretending that the loss did not hurt. It can coexist with sorrow, uncertainty, and the gradual process of rebuilding your life.

If you are experiencing grief and would like support, I encourage you to consider therapy and reach out to determine whether it may be a good fit for you. Counseling can provide a supportive space to process what happened, understand your grief, and explore what moving forward can look like for you. Give us a call today to schedule an appointment.

item.title: Freeing Yourself from Parental Codependency
item.description:
Codependency is a toxic trait that ultimately drains the life out of any relationship, causing long-term emotional damage to all participants. Though you might not even know what codependency is or how to identify it, you will still feel the effects of it.

Codependent people make you feel trapped and responsible for their stability and contentment, often while contributing little in return. Most people have the option of limiting the influence of a codependent person in their lives, but what do you do when the codependent person in your life is a parent? Parental codependency is more difficult to diagnose and navigate, especially when you want to maintain a relationship with your parent.

Parental codependency is when a parent looks to their child or children to fulfill all of their emotional needs. It is parenting in reverse, with the child being forced to act as the parent. Although codependent parents are often manipulative, controlling, and emotionally immature, they also thrive on making you feel as if they are your best friend.

For this reason, and many others, it can take years to realize that your parent was codependent and that you were affected by years of emotional neglect and manipulation. It is only when someone can validate your experience that you can begin to heal emotionally and untangle yourself from parental codependency.

Unfulfilled Needs

Every parent is affected by the way they were parented. Some grew up in healthy homes, and some in toxic ones. More often than not, a person’s childhood is a combination of good, bad, and neutral. Most parents try their best and still get it wrong occasionally.

At the core of parental codependency is a history of needs that were neglected, ignored, or unseen. The emptiness that comes from emotional neglect doesn’t go away. Most people try to fulfill those unmet needs in relationships, including those within their family.

As the saying goes, you can’t give what you don’t have. Within every codependent parent, there is a deficit of affection, attention, acceptance, or affirmation. If a person’s practical, emotional, and developmental needs were never met by their parents, they will naturally struggle to fulfill their children’s needs. This explains parental codependency, but it doesn’t excuse it.

What Parental Codependency Feels Like

A codependent parent engineers family life to revolve around themselves. Like the main character, they demand focus, make demands, and take up all the emotional space in their family’s life. Not every codependent parent is obnoxious in the way they control and manipulate their children. Parental codependency makes it seem like your parent is your best friend.

In childhood, a codependent parent often reduces their child’s access to alone time and privacy, enforcing rules like having no closed doors in the house and carefully monitoring all of their children’s interactions with friends. It can be difficult to identify a codependent parent because they look like an attentive or involved parent.

The strict rules and structure they enforce are self-serving, though, as they are simply trying to control and stay connected to their children at any cost. It’s not unusual for a codependent parent to view their child’s extra-curricular activities, their friends, new relationships, or hobbies and interests as threats that must be controlled.

Many codependent parents remain attached to their adult children, too. Without being able to enforce rules anymore, they might shift tactics, becoming more manipulative to get their way. They might guilt-trip their children into making daily phone calls and make regular check-ins and visits.

Even when a codependent parent tries to foster the feeling of being your best friend, it often feels threatening and emotionally suffocating. Though it is typically unspoken, you know that you are expected to prioritize their needs and work according to their timetable.

Freeing Yourself from Parental Codependency

When you are in a relationship with someone who is always taking from you and never giving back, you will come to resent that person and do whatever it takes to sever ties with them. Sometimes, however, it is too complex to sever a relationship with a codependent parent. There comes a point where enough is enough, however, and you will need to decide how to calibrate the relationship.

If you grew up in a home affected by parental codependency, you likely never got a good example of what healthy parenting looks like. Even the media often portrays unhealthy parenting models for the sake of entertainment. These examples are so prevalent that it’s easy to think they’re the norm, especially when they align with your experience. You first need to unravel the toxic dynamics that have defined your relationship with your parent.

In a healthy model of parenthood, the child needs the parent, and the parent knows this. In parental codependency, the parent needs the child, and the child slowly becomes aware of this over time. A codependent parent will feel threatened and panicked whenever you pull away or enforce a boundary. Conversely, a healthy parent celebrates your growing independence and cheers you on from the sidelines.

It’s important to know what is and what isn’t healthy parenting. This is especially true if you have been the victim of emotional neglect, manipulation, and gaslighting your entire life. Step one of freeing yourself from parental codependency is realizing what is and what isn’t acceptable in your relationship with your parent.

Children of codependent parents often feel invisible because their needs were never met, their dreams and goals never encouraged, and their experiences never validated. A vital step in liberating and healing from parental codependency is processing your thoughts and experiences with someone who will listen and help explain the codependency in your relationship.

You can share with a friend, partner, or therapist. Keep in mind that your parent will not likely respond positively if you were to open up. They would likely become defensive and go into attack mode, potentially adding to the damage they’ve already caused.

One of the most cathartic things you could do as someone who grew up with a codependent parent is flipping the script and being the one to make the rules. You’ll likely encounter a lot of resistance from your parent, and some emotional backlash, but you will only begin to recover from parental codependency when you begin enforcing boundaries.

As an adult, you get to determine how much involvement and support you are willing to provide to your parent. Simply telling them “No” is as effective a boundary as any. You might have to contend with feelings of guilt, but boundaries become easier to enforce when you are consistent in your efforts. It is important to know you can still honor your parent as Scripture requires while still holding healthy boundaries.

Some relationships are so damaged and have caused so much damage that they cannot be mended. Codependent people are unlikely to take their share of the responsibility to fix a relationship, leaving you to do all the work as you have always done. It’s a serious thing to stop all of your efforts and allow a relationship to die, especially when it is with a parent. However, sometimes it is the only option that will allow you and your family to be free and begin healing.

You can recover from parental codependency if you become aware of how your codependent parent has affected you in the past, and how they continue to affect you. Speak with someone who will validate your experiences and maintain consistent boundaries when interacting with your parent. You are not doomed to repeat your parents’ failures, regardless of what you have experienced up until now.

If you would like to begin processing your experiences with a counselor, please don’t hesitate to reach out to the office. There is an online catalog of counselors where you can find someone suitable to meet with. Alternatively, you can speak with the reception team, who will be happy to connect you with a counselor to meet your needs.

item.title: What is Grief? What to Expect in Each of the Stages of Grief and Loss
item.description:
We all have many different life experiences that make us unique. However, if we live long enough, grief is a shared experience many of us carry. Grief can be described as a response to loss. This usually involves the death of someone, but it can also include other losses such as divorce, loss of a home or job, or loss of health or independence.

Grief is normal and healthy

Grief is a normal and healthy response to loss. We might have grown up with the idea that grieving is abnormal and unhealthy (real men don’t cry), but this just isn’t true. God designed us to love and care deeply, and the response to losing those we love is grief.

Not only is it normal, but it’s also healthy. When we refuse to grieve, we actually cause ourselves harm. It’s like a balloon. We can only stuff so much air into a balloon before it pops. We are like that with our emotions. We can only “stuff” our feelings so much before we pop, too.

We might explode in anger, experience depression, or even experience physical symptoms such as stomach problems or headaches. Also, unresolved grief can build upon itself when we experience the next grief. When we choose to sweep things under the rug, we are just causing ourselves more work and agony the next time we experience loss.

When we grieve, we not only grieve the loss of the person, but we mourn the loss of the roles, dreams, nuances, and routines that went along with our relationship with them. These are called secondary losses. Roles include parts the loved one played that will possibly need to be passed on to others. Some examples of this are the “fun one”, tech guy, party planner, banker, cook, etc.

We experience a loss of dreams and expectations, such as the deceased person not being able to be there when grandchildren are born. More subtle things include the way a person smells, physical touch such as sleeping in the same bed, etc. There are also many changes in routine when we lose someone. This might include having Thanksgiving at someone else’s house or changing from a couple’s Sunday school class to a women’s or men’s class.

Everyone grieves differently. This is based on many factors such as personality, type of death, our relationship with them, support systems, etc. For instance, an individual would normally grieve the peaceful passing of their ninety-year-old grandmother differently than their child suddenly being killed in a car accident.

The type of death and circumstances surrounding it often have a major impact. Sometimes a good relationship with the deceased makes their death harder, but a rocky, estranged relationship can also make grieving difficult.

The Five Stages Grieving Model

One common grief model puts typical grieving into five stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. Let’s look at what we might expect from each stage.

Denial

Denial usually happens when we first learn about the loss. It can include shock, numbness, confusion, and fear. Our bodies and minds cannot process the news we have just received, and it is hard to believe what has happened. It can be a protective coping mechanism that helps us get through those first few weeks. It helps us be able to plan funerals and make lots of hard decisions.

Often people will wake up from sleep and wonder if the loss really happened or if it was just a dream. It might cause us to walk into that person’s house and briefly look for them or call them, forgetting that they aren’t there to answer. Sometimes people are concerned that they don’t have much emotion in the beginning. All of these are common in the first stage.

Anger

Anger is common in the grieving process and can be directed at many different people. We might be angry with ourselves for not doing something differently or spending enough time with them. We might be angry with a doctor or the driver who caused a car accident. We might be angry with God for allowing this terrible thing to happen. We might even be angry with the deceased for not taking better care of themself or for how they treated us.

Sometimes we’re angry because we had such a good relationship with them, and sometimes we’re angry because it was a traumatic or difficult relationship. Anger is often described as a secondary emotion, meaning we’re never “just angry.” We experience anger because of some other emotion such as pain, embarrassment, or guilt. We experience many varied emotions when we grieve, and they often come out as anger.

Bargaining

This takes place when we have “if only” thinking. “If only we didn’t go on vacation.” “If only we had seen the doctor sooner.” We use magical thinking to try to undo something that happened. We often experience guilt in this phase. We blame ourselves for the death, thinking somehow we could have prevented it.

We wish we had spent more time or said certain things. We spend lots of time longing for the person to come back and grasp at anything to try to undo what has happened. We know logically this is futile, but it is a natural part of grief.

Depression

This can take many forms. Of course we feel sad, but it usually goes deeper than that. We might experience physical symptoms such as headaches, pain, or stomach problems. We might not be able to sleep or sleep too much. We might not enjoy doing things that used to bring us joy. Difficulty concentrating and making decisions is also difficult during this phase. We can feel like we’re in a fog, or our brain just won’t work right.

Isolation from others is often common. Part of us knows we should and need to get out and be around friends, but we just don’t want to. Sometimes it’s because we feel sad, and sometimes it’s how we perceive others at this time. We might be angry that people didn’t reach out to us in the way or as frequently as we wanted. Sometimes we are aggravated that people won’t leave us alone.

People often don’t know how to act around the grieving person or what to say to them. They often say foolish and unintentionally hurtful things. “They’re in a better place.” “You should be thankful your dad lived that long.” Others are uncomfortable and feel the need to fill the silence with ill-thought-out words.

This hurts and frustrates us and makes us feel like others just don’t understand. Sometimes they avoid the grieving person or avoid the elephant in the room because they don’t know what to say or do. All of these can cause isolation and hurt. It’s also easy to have irrational thinking and be oversensitive during this time.

Acceptance

Acceptance is the final stage of grief. It is the opposite of bargaining or longing for what was lost. We finally accept the reality that our loved one is no longer here. While we never truly get over the loss, we learn to live with it. It becomes our new normal and is a sense of finality.

Often, those who have moved on to the acceptance phase of grief desire to give back to others. It helps them make sense of the loss by turning it into something good. This can include giving money in the person’s name for a cause, leading a grief group, or bringing a meal to a person who has just experienced loss.

Often people want to know how long the grieving process lasts. Unfortunately, there is no time limit or date on the calendar when it will be over. Some experts say grief lasts about two years, but that can depend on a lot of factors. The first year will be hard because we have to experience all the “firsts”: first Christmas, first birthday, and the anniversary of their death. These are often hard days for several years.

Next Steps

Grieving is one of the hardest events we can experience in life. There isn’t a pill to take or a procedure to hurry it up. We have to give ourselves time and permission to grieve. Grief takes time, but it also takes work.

If you feel you are struggling with your grief, don’t go it alone. Talk to a counselor or grief group to walk with you through this difficult time. They can give you a safe place to express your thoughts, memories, and emotions and help you work through this painful process.

item.title: The Roles of Mind, Self, and Brain in Healing Depression: Learning to Stay Out of the River of Our Negative Cognitions
item.description:
Depression occurs when stressful life events influence the brain. These events create more negative thoughts and feelings and more distortion in the way the brain processes information. To understand this process is it is important to realize that the human brain consists of three distinct components which have a role in the management of depression.

Three Components of Depression Management

The first component, which we will identify, is the mind, located in the anterior cingulate gyrus. The mind is the stream or river of consciousness through which flow thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations. It is not the source of the content of the river; it is a conduit for processing the content.

The second component is the Self, located in the prefrontal cortex, on the bank of the mind or river of consciousness. This component is our sense of “I”, the internal executor of the brain, and in a real sense, this is where our soul resides, called our “heart” in the Scriptures.

The Self could observe the thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations which flow through the mind and process them. The Self observes the contents of the river, but they are not the same as the mind.

Just because a thought enters the river, it doesn’t mean you have to believe it – the Self determines the validity of the contents of the river. The limbic system of the brain is the source of the contents of the river – thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations. Remember, the brain is not the same component as the mind.

How the Brain Processes Information

The brain produces the stream of thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations by processing information from:

  • The real world
  • Your body and senses, including your gut
  • By recalling past packages of thoughts, feelings, beliefs, and motor/action plans or schemas that make sense of our experiences

For example, you see a plant while on a hike, and you’ve never seen one like it before. It might be a green leafy plant, but you’ve never seen this kind before. What is it? The automatic systems in your brain take over and process this real-world information with the anxiety you are feeling in your body and gut, as you are concerned this might actually be poison ivy, because you have heard there might be some around.

The brain then starts recalling things from your past. This plant has three leaves like the one you touched when you were a kid, so it sends anxiety and danger signals down the river. But these automatic functions only control 80% of your brain. The other 5-20 % come from the Self. So, you have some executor options. You can become overwhelmed by what the brain is sending, believe it, and jump in the river, or you can analyze and appraise.

You can say things like, yes, there might be poison ivy plants around, but they do not have leaves like the one I saw as a kid. Yes, poison ivy can cause problems, but didn’t that plant hurt me when I was a kid because I plucked it up? Have any of my friends had a problem with poison ivy on this trail?

The Brain and the Self

The brain is an organ, just like the gut or the heart. Sometimes it cooperates fully with the rest of the body, and sometimes it doesn’t. If you allow negative things into your brain, i.e., pornography, violent video games or movies, abuse, it will react negatively. You are not your brain, but you can change your brain.

Negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations sent into the river by the brain are observed by the Self, which is safely located on the bank in the real world, where it can reappraise after stepping back and seeing the situation clearly.

The problem develops when the Self becomes entangled in the river by ruminating on the thoughts and feelings it encounters there. You (Self) become the negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations. This rumination results in a new reality. The Self, who is stuck in the river, creates a new thought: “My brain is telling me this, so it must be true!”

The result of this new reality is an overwhelming sense of sadness, lack of motivation, and loss of interest in things we formerly enjoyed. The Self is stuck in negative thoughts. One of the consequences of the Self being stuck in the river is that the prefrontal cortex is turned off and is not working as designed. The solution to the problem lies in learning to redirect attention to the real world through mindfulness techniques and cognitive restructuring.

Mindfulness

Mindfulness is keeping our thoughts in the present, where it is safe, and not in the past, which is dominated by “If onlys”, or the future, which is dominated by “What ifs.” Cognitive restructuring is challenging the validity and logic of the negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations, using the logical prefrontal cortex where the Self resides.

The safest place to direct attention is to the real world, not the river. If we fall into the river, we drown in depression. So, the question you need to ask yourself is, “Is there anything happening right here, right now in this room with which you cannot deal or handle?”

Healing depression focuses on climbing out of the river by remembering the scriptural admonition to claim the promise of Philippians 4:7, and receive the peace of God, which the Apostle Paul states, “…Surpasses all understanding, and will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Phil. 4:7 ESV).

If we can learn not to live in the past or worry about the future, but instead to learn from the past and apply the lessons learned, we can face the future assured of the strength of the Lord to guide us. And in the process, we allow the Self to resume the executor role of the brain as God designed it, and we stay grounded in the present in the real world.

Research has shown that the Brain has the capacity to stay in the present for 4-7 seconds before it starts to wander to the past or future. Consequently, we need to empower the Self, steal that attention away from the brain, and mindfully bring it back to the present.

We accomplish this with in-the-moment coping skills, such as diaphragmatic breathing, mindfulness techniques that activate prefrontal cortex activity, and challenging the validity and logic of negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations.

Challenging Negative Thoughts

We can systematically challenge each negative thought, each negative feeling, each troubling image, and each sensation by identifying what percentage they are true. At first, we might think they are 90-100% true, and that’s what keeps us in the river. But the Self, which is watching from the riverbank, can see that the reality is that the percentage is much, much lower. A common example is “I can never do anything right!” and it is believed 100%.

But hearing the Self challenge the statement with the logic that no one is always wrong, and everyone does some things right, lowers the percentage substantially and starts on the path to healing. Allowing the Self to put the negatives on trial, and asking, “What is the evidence that I should believe this?”, is another effective way to climb out of the river.

In conclusion, don’t forget that living in the “If onlys” of the past and the “What ifs” of the future will cause the brain to convince us that there is no hope. When we get the Self and the prefrontal cortex involved in the challenging process, we can claim the promise that healing and peace are only a prayer away!

So, if you feel you are drowning in the river of your negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations, please know there is hope through a therapist who understands the healing process. Please check our website and make an appointment today. Peace awaits.

item.title: What is Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD)?
item.description:
We have all seen it before – a social media friend posts a picture of their perfectly color-coded closet. Their pantry is organized into matching containers. Every towel is folded exactly the same way. The caption reads: “#OCD.”

Or maybe you’ve seen someone look at a crooked picture frame or a stack of papers that isn’t perfectly straight and joke, “My OCD is going so crazy right now.” Most of us have laughed, nodded, or kept scrolling without thinking much about it.

But what if OCD is actually something completely different? What if the person silently battling Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder has a messy closet, an overflowing laundry basket, and a mind that never gives them a moment of peace?

The truth is that OCD has little to do with being neat, organized, or particular. It is a disorder driven by fear. It is a disorder built on uncertainty. And for those living with it, it can feel like you are battling a monster on steroids every single day.

Why OCD Thoughts Cause So Much Distress

One of the most difficult parts of OCD is that people often mistake intrusive thoughts for who they are.

An intrusive thought is exactly what it sounds like: an unwanted thought, image, or urge that repeatedly barges into your mind without your permission. These thoughts are distressing because they are the exact thoughts you do not want to have. If you could snap your fingers and make them disappear forever, you would.

Ironically, the harder you try to force them away, argue with them, or prove they are not true, the longer they tend to stick around. This is one of the reasons OCD is so exhausting. These types of thoughts are often referred to as “sticky thoughts” (also referred to as obsessions).

Everyone experiences random intrusive thoughts from time to time. A person who isn’t battling OCD may briefly notice the thought and move on with their day. Their brain simply lets it pass.

But someone dealing with OCD tends to get stuck. The thought lingers, replaying over and over. It may stay for hours or even days, demanding attention and creating tremendous anxiety. The brain becomes convinced that the thought must mean something important simply because it won’t leave.

People might think:

“What if I secretly want this?”
“What if this thought means something about me?”
“What if God is trying to tell me something?”
“What if everyone else is safe except me?”

However, the opposite is usually true. OCD likes to attack what matters most to us. A loving mother may develop terrifying thoughts about accidentally harming her child. A devoted Christian might become consumed with fears that they have committed an unforgivable sin or will in the future.

A compassionate person may become terrified that they could harm someone else, or even themselves, despite desperately not wanting to. Someone who deeply values honesty becomes trapped wondering if they lied without realizing it.

Deep down, people battling with OCD might even recognize that these thoughts are attacking the values they hold most dear. If a thought fills you with fear because it goes completely against who you are and what you believe, that is often evidence that it is not something you actually want to do. OCD doesn’t reveal your character. Instead, it attacks your values.

Could I be dealing with OCD?

If you’ve been reading this article and wondering whether this could apply to you, here are some common symptoms of OCD.

OCD may be the culprit if you:

  • Experience recurring intrusive thoughts, images, or urges that feel unwanted and distressing.
  • Spend a significant amount of time trying to figure out what your thoughts mean.
  • Constantly seek reassurance from others that everything is okay.
  • Feel driven to check, repeat, confess, avoid, or perform mental rituals to reduce anxiety.
  • Feel temporary relief after completing a compulsion, only to have the fear return later.
  • Find yourself avoiding people, places, objects, or situations that trigger intrusive thoughts.
  • Spend an hour or more each day consumed by obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors.
  • Notice that the anxiety is interfering with your work, relationships, parenting, school, or ability to enjoy life.

It is important to remember that everyone experiences intrusive thoughts from time to time. Having an intrusive thought does not necessarily mean you are dealing with OCD. The difference is how your brain responds to the thought. For someone who isn’t fighting OCD, the thought usually comes and goes without much attention.

For someone who is facing OCD, the thought can become “sticky.” The brain treats it like an emergency that must be solved immediately. This is where compulsions may develop. But, the more you try to make the thought go away, the stronger it often becomes. This only makes the cycles stronger.

If this cycle sounds familiar, know that you are not alone. OCD affects millions of people, and many go years before receiving an accurate diagnosis because they don’t realize what they’re experiencing has a name.

There is hope

If you recognized yourself in this article, know that OCD is highly treatable. You do not have to stay trapped in the exhausting cycle of obsessions (sticky thoughts) and/or compulsions (behaviors you adopt to relieve the anxiety you feel).

Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a specialized form of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), is the gold-standard treatment for OCD. Rather than trying to eliminate intrusive thoughts, ERP helps you change your response to them so they gradually lose their power.

Recovery doesn’t mean you’ll never have another intrusive thought. It means those thoughts no longer control your life.

If you’re struggling with OCD or intrusive thoughts, I’d love to help. Reach out today to schedule an appointment and learn how evidence-based treatment can help you break free from OCD and regain peace.

item.title: How Emotionally-Focused Marriage Therapy Can Help Couples Facing Chronic Disease
item.description:
For someone dealing with a sudden diagnosis or finally discovering what’s beneath their health issues, chronic disease is difficult. Whether the newly diagnosed person receives the news in a way that alters their self-perception or it is slowly revealed through life’s limitations, chronic health issues take their toll. Not only is it hard for the individual experiencing them, but they can be damaging to a marriage.

If you or someone you love is dealing with chronic illness or a new diagnosis that impacts the rest of their life, it may be wise to seek emotionally focused marriage therapy as another tool for your well-being toolkit.

Here’s why:

Marriages facing additional layers of complexity need more complex layers of support. Marriage is hard no matter what. But when one partner is diagnosed with a life-threatening illness or a disease that significantly impacts the family, it adds more stress to the relationship. With about 41% of first marriages ending in divorce, even without chronic health issues, it’s important to arm yourself with as many wellness tools as you can.

What is emotionally focused marriage therapy?

According to the International Center for Excellence in Emotionally Focused Therapy (ICEEFT), couples counseling rooted in emotionally focused therapy takes “an evidence-based approach to psychotherapy, drawing primarily from attachment theory to facilitate the creation of secure, vibrant connection with self and others.”

It’s a means of helping couples identify where they’re attached insecurely, learn new ways of attaching to one another that bring life and health back to the marriage, and approach problem-solving and plans from the emotionally focused lens they’ve developed in their sessions.

Emotionally focused marriage therapy has three phases: De-escalation, Restructuring, and Consolidation.

In de-escalation, a couple explores what “broke” the healthy attachments they once had. If they didn’t develop these healthy attachments, they will explore what might contribute to that. Often, there are cycles that a couple can recognize that explain why they have had the same fight for years and didn’t know how to solve it.

With restructuring, a couple learns new ways to listen, be open to each other, and express their needs. Both partners can be available to the other person’s needs in a way that feels authentic yet invites vulnerability. This builds a foundation of trust and safety that the lack of attachment did not previously contain.

The third phase, consolidation, helps the couple recognize how their new tools can be useful in the future. Particularly with couples facing chronic illness, this phase is crucial to helping them reflect on ways they can partner together to use the therapeutic listening and engaging they’ve learned as they cope with the emotional upheaval that chronic illness can create.

How can this therapy help us with chronic health diagnoses?

When one partner receives life-changing health news, it’s challenging to embrace. But then, the steady impact over time becomes a “new normal” that their spouse needs to receive, and if not, this can disrupt the marital connection.

It can also create levels of feeling unseen or unsupported, especially if the partner with the illness doesn’t feel cared for. No matter how much their spouse wants to show support, they may simply not be equipped to show it in a way that communicates support the way their partner needs.

Even doctors miss this sometimes, so it’s natural that a spouse trying to support their spouse who’s facing chronic health issues may not know how to do it well. Emotions run high on both sides, fear can enter the picture even for the most confident couples, and security may go out the proverbial window.

So, a counselor trained in emotionally focused marriage therapy can be a godsend to couples who just don’t know what to do next. They’ve made the physical health decisions (or some of them anyway) about medications, treatments, and lifestyle changes. But when it comes to the emotional side of it? That’s a layer that can feel too burdensome to tackle with the physical health decisions as well.

Your EFT counselor will help by letting you practice the therapy in the actual sessions. He or she will guide you through each phase, so you can see that you don’t have to “do” anything except listen to the counselor, talk honestly, and have a willing heart. A willingness to understand your spouse during this stressful time goes a long way.

In counseling, you’ll learn the ineffective ways your communication, expression of emotions, and actions toward each other impact the relationship’s harmony and sense of safety. The counselor will also teach you how to recognize your feelings, fears, and anything else serving as barriers to connection to each other during this season.

An Example of How EFT Fuels Conversation in Couple Therapy

Here’s an example from one research study about how a cancer patient’s diagnosis can move from panic and stress-inducing to peaceful and comfort-building in their relationship. Let’s suppose one partner is diagnosed with cancer.

When the shock of the diagnosis has subsided somewhat, the person’s partner may want to discuss treatment options, what-if scenarios, and how to maximize support. The partner may be so fearful of outcomes that they avoid these discussions.

The success of those conversations (or avoidances) can have a direct impact on emotional health. Still, some studies show that even a person’s physical recovery time can be reduced if their partner can provide the kind of support they need.

A counselor who specializes in emotionally focused couple therapy may meet with the couple to discern (in phase one) which cycles are playing a role in their discussions about the newfound diagnosis. Through a conversation they have in session, a counselor may gently ask a reflective question to the person experiencing the illness: How does it make you feel when you talk about cancer and your spouse changes the subject?

The couple can practice navigating their feelings, being open with one another, and learning (with the counselor’s guidance) to listen to each other’s needs with empathy. Over time, this transitions them to phase two, where the learned experience transforms how they provide support to one another.

What they discover, then, is that they each have significant needs; no one partner’s needs are “more important” than the other. That way, they learn how to value one another’s feelings, express themselves with gentleness, and receive feedback so they can talk more openly and with kindness, compassion, and even humor.

Couples who navigate through health challenges with these communication styles tend to walk away from the challenges feeling more connected to their partner than before.

While emotionally focused therapy doesn’t focus on skill development like cognitive behavioral therapy would, it does incorporate learning in a flexible, felt-need way. This fluid approach to seeing and hearing each other in therapy sessions with a guide can provide a sense of comfort to the partner who may be resistant to therapy at first.

What to Expect in Emotionally Focused Marriage Therapy Session One

First, recognize that it is common not to want to attend therapy. Usually at least one partner – if not both – is hesitant. Hesitation can come from a host of attitudes, feelings, and beliefs about what marriage therapy involves.

Second, both partners should be aware that the first session is not a long-term commitment. You’re simply going to share what fueled the idea. It’s not a blame game; it’s pragmatics. One of you was diagnosed with a chronic illness or disease, and you’d like a little help navigating how you’re both coping with the news. It can be simple and fact-driven. You don’t need to be ready to bear your soul or even understand how you’re feeling.

Third, the counselor who specializes in emotionally focused marriage therapy understands not just how to ask questions but also how to hold space for someone who may be grieving, disassociated from what’s happening, feeling ignored or left out, or a variety of other hard realities.

If anything, a counselor looking at therapy from an EFT lens will be more inclined to affirm where you are right now. You’ll walk away with hope – and that’s often reason enough to attend just one session.

Finally, it can be a mutual decision after you’ve attended session one about whether you think it will benefit you both. Listening to the counselor and sharing a bit of your story from an overview level won’t repair anyone overnight; however, it can give you an idea of whether you’ll each get something out of a second session.

If you or your spouse, or someone else in your lives, would benefit from emotionally focused marriage therapy, we are here for you. Contact one of our offices to be matched with a counselor in your area.
